# OWASP Dependency-Check

This example examines a software-supply-chain trust boundary: Maven resolves
third-party artifacts from repositories and the application includes them on its
runtime classpath. The application does not control the security state of those
components merely because its own source code is small.

The unsafe baseline pins Log4j 2.15.0, a version with high-severity known
vulnerabilities. Its failure mode is that a vulnerable component can progress
through a normal build unless the build evaluates the dependency graph against
vulnerability intelligence. The exercise compares that baseline with a newer
version while OWASP Dependency-Check enforces a CVSS threshold. The dependency
versions and scanner results are workshop evidence, not production approval.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- identify the Maven dependency-resolution and runtime-classpath trust boundary;
- trace the vulnerable Log4j version and Dependency-Check policy in the POM;
- demonstrate that the vulnerable dependency fails the configured build gate and
  verify the result with the generated report; and
- explain why updating one version is not sufficient without ongoing review of
  findings, suppressions, and release policy.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25 or newer](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- Internet access is required when Dependency-Check updates its local
  vulnerability database. The Maven Wrapper is included, so a separate Maven
  installation is not required.
- A web browser is required only to inspect the generated local HTML report.
- An NVD API key is optional but recommended for repeated scans. If available,
  export it as `NVD_API_KEY`; the POM reads that environment variable. Do not
  place the key in the POM, command history, or source control.

## The program to inspect

`Main` does not process untrusted application input. It only loads Log4j and
writes a message. That contrast is deliberate: the relevant attack surface is
the third-party component selected by the build, rather than complex Java logic.

```java
package demo;

import org.apache.logging.log4j.LogManager;
import org.apache.logging.log4j.Logger;

/**
 * Hello world!
 */
public final class Main {

    private static final Logger LOGGER = LogManager.getLogger(Main.class);

    public static void main(final String[] args) {
        LOGGER.info("Hello there!");
    }
}
```

The POM centralises the Log4j version. The vulnerable baseline is explicit, so
attendees can compare a newer version without rewriting the dependency graph.

```xml
<properties>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    <java.version>25</java.version>
    <maven.compiler.release>${java.version}</maven.compiler.release>

    <!-- Change this value to a remediated release to compare scanner results. -->
    <log4j2.version>2.15.0</log4j2.version>
    <junit.version>6.1.3</junit.version>
```

Dependency-Check runs the `check` goal during the Maven build. It reads the NVD
API key only from the `NVD_API_KEY` environment variable and fails the build at
the configured CVSS threshold. The threshold is a policy decision, not a
universal definition of acceptable risk.

```xml
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.owasp</groupId>
    <artifactId>dependency-check-maven</artifactId>
    <version>${dependency-check.version}</version>
    <configuration>
        <failBuildOnCVSS>${dependency-check.failBuildOnCVSS}</failBuildOnCVSS>
        <nvdApiKey>${env.NVD_API_KEY}</nvdApiKey>
        <ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>false</ossIndexAnalyzerEnabled>
    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>check</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>
```

## Guided walkthrough

Run these commands from this example directory. They create local Maven and
`target/` artifacts, and the scanner can update its local vulnerability cache.
They do not change system configuration. NVD data and CVE matches change over
time, so inspect the current report rather than treating the listed version or a
cached result as a permanent security verdict.

1. Run the scanner against the intentionally vulnerable baseline.

   The first run may take longer while Dependency-Check downloads or updates
   vulnerability data. A build failure is expected because the configured
   threshold is 8. The report is the evidence to inspect, not an approval
   decision.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check
   ```

2. Inspect the generated report.

   Confirm the affected dependency, CVEs, whether each finding is direct or
   transitive, and whether the CVSS threshold matches your team's policy. Open
   the local report in a browser if you want its full detail.

   ```shell
   ls -l 'target/dependency-check-report.html'
   ```

   The report is generated locally at `target/dependency-check-report.html`.
   Opening it is a manual review step; do not automatically trust a suppression,
   scanner match, or successful report generation.

3. Run the normal Maven `verify` lifecycle.

   This confirms that the policy is part of the normal build rather than a
   one-off command. It is expected to fail for the vulnerable baseline and to
   leave the report available for review.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean verify
   ```
